issues.failure_explanation: The displayed asymptotic quotient is inapplicable when its leading denominator coefficient vanishes. In particular, C=D=0 satisfies C+D=0, but the exact formula gives G(z)=[1+z(1/6+(2/3)R(z))]/(1-z/6), so R(z) tends to 1 and G(z) tends to -5, not 0.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Exclude C=D=0 and handle all cases where the leading denominator coefficient vanishes directly before stating the corrected equivalence.
issues.overall_effect: The lemma's stated equivalence is false at the degenerate parameter pair, although the later positive-C parameter range avoids that pair.
issues.title: Zero-parameter exception invalidates the claimed iff condition
issues.why_classification: A short exceptional-case analysis corrects the lemma without changing the final positive-C scheme or its advertised parameter range.

issues.failure_explanation: For C<0, the product of the two roots of the quadratic is 2/(3C)<0. Hence the roots are real with opposite signs, so one lies in the left half-plane. The quoted expression is only their average real part when the roots form a conjugate pair; it is not the real part of each root in the negative-C case.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the root argument by the quadratic sign or Routh-Hurwitz test and restrict the stated regime to C>=0, with C=0 treated separately.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed analyticity regime C<-1/39 is false. The later selected interval with C>0 is not affected by this particular error.
issues.title: Pole-location lemma incorrectly includes negative C
issues.why_classification: The correction locally removes an unused negative-parameter branch while preserving the final positive-parameter method.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Analytically proving $\lvert G(iy)\rvert\leq 1$ for all $y\in\mathbb{R}$ is complex. Instead, we employ a systematic numerical scanning algorithm to determine the A-stability conditions of the scheme.

The parameter space $C \in [0.00, 0.10]$ is discretized into 5,000 sampling points, while the frequency domain along the imaginary axis $y\in [10^{-8}, 10^{4}]$ is densely sampled using 25,000 logarithmically spaced points.

issues.failure_explanation: A finite scan cannot prove the required supremum over all real y and all C in a continuum. More decisively, algebra from the paper's rational G gives |denominator(iy)|^2-|numerator(iy)|^2 = y^6[-(1-75C+1170C^2)/3456+(C^2/1024)y^2]. Thus stability near y=0 requires 1170C^2-75C+1<=0, namely C between (75-sqrt(945))/2340 approximately 0.0189142 and (75+sqrt(945))/2340 approximately 0.0451884. Both stated endpoints extend into unstable regions.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the finite-scan inference with an analytic imaginary-axis inequality and correct the interval to the exact admissible range, while retaining the pole analysis for analyticity.
issues.overall_effect: The formal A-stability conclusion and the assertion that every final scheme with C in the displayed interval is A-stable are false as written.
issues.title: The claimed A-stability interval contains unstable parameters
issues.why_classification: A comparable A-stability result appears recoverable, but it requires a nontrivial analytic argument and materially changes the advertised parameter interval.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For each parameter-frequency pair $(C, y)$, the corresponding amplification factor $\lvert G(iy)\rvert$ is computed. The algorithm identifies the maximum amplification factor across all frequencies and verifies its compliance with the stability criterion $\lvert G(iy)\rvert \leq1$.

issues.failure_explanation: The scan described only tests compliance with |G(iy)|<=1; it defines no damping objective whose optimizer is 0.018924. Moreover, the maximum over the imaginary axis is at least |G(0)|=1 for every consistent method, and under the imposed condition all admitted nonzero C also have G(infinity)=0, so neither stated quantity singles out this parameter.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Define a mathematically meaningful damping functional and prove or numerically resolve its optimization over the corrected stable interval, or withdraw the optimality claim.
issues.overall_effect: The designation of C=0.018924 as optimal and its claimed superior damping are unsupported, even after correcting the A-stability interval.
issues.title: The claimed optimal damping parameter has no defined or established optimization criterion
issues.why_classification: Preserving the optimality promise requires a new criterion and a contained reoptimization; otherwise the paper must relinquish that substantive claim.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Implicit Runge-Kutta methods proposed by Kuntzmann \cite{Kuntzmann-1961} and Butcher \cite{Butcher-1964}, such as Radau and Gauss-type schemes, compute slopes at future time steps by solving systems of nonlinear equations.

issues.failure_explanation: There is no unique fourth-order implicit Runge-Kutta method, and the source itself mentions distinct Radau and Gauss families. No Butcher tableau, stage equations, or other identifying definition is supplied, so the comparator underlying every 'Implicit RK4' error column is undefined and the quantitative comparison cannot be reproduced or assessed.

failure_location.quote: Additionally, a direct comparison is conducted between the proposed implicit TSFO scheme and the classical fourth-order implicit Runge-Kutta (e.g., Implicit RK4) method, focusing on stable time step size and convergence error, to verify the superiority of the former.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Specify the exact implicit Runge-Kutta tableau and nonlinear-solve settings used and rerun or verify all comparator data; alternatively remove the comparative claims and columns.
issues.overall_effect: All numerical error and stability comparisons against 'Implicit RK4' lack a specified mathematical baseline.
issues.title: The implicit Runge-Kutta comparator is not mathematically specified
issues.why_classification: Repairing the comparison requires identifying the method and validating a substantial collection of numerical results, while withdrawal would cause a limited but material loss of the competitiveness claim.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
This problem is described by the following
eight-dimensional system:

$L^2$-Norm Error and Convergence Order Analysis of Implicit TSFO and Implicit RK4 Methods for

"Ozone Decomposition Reaction Problem" with $t_{\text{end}}=1.0$.

issues.failure_explanation: The eight-dimensional initial-value problem gives no value for u_7(0). Consequently it does not determine a unique solution, and the source does not identify which problem generated the six ozone error tables.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply the actual value of u_7(0) used and verify the tables for that complete initial condition, or remove the ozone benchmark from the validation claims.
issues.overall_effect: The ozone benchmark and its convergence results are not reproducible or mathematically tied to the stated initial-value problem.
issues.title: The ozone benchmark omits an initial condition
issues.why_classification: The missing value is not forced by the source; preserving the benchmark requires recovering and checking its input, while withdrawal loses one substantial validation case.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Numerical results confirm that the proposed two-step fourth-order implicit (Implicit TSFO) scheme effectively solves stiff problems using large time steps without compromising fourth-order accuracy. When compared to the classical implicit Runge-Kutta (Implicit RK4) method, our scheme reduces the numerical error by about an order of magnitude under identical time steps and offers superior stability that enables even larger step sizes.

issues.failure_explanation: The numerical tables contain only TSFO and an unspecified implicit-RK comparator; they contain no explicit-RK results. They also use identical listed time steps rather than determining stability thresholds or comparing stability regions. Error differences at common steps do not establish that TSFO permits larger stable steps.

failure_location.quote: Comparisons with classical explicit and implicit fourth-order Runge-Kutta methods demonstrate that the proposed scheme possesses superior stability regions and smaller numerical errors.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add specified explicit and implicit RK comparators together with stability-boundary or maximum-stable-step experiments, or narrow the conclusions to the common-step error comparisons actually presented.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised experimental demonstration of superiority over explicit RK methods and of larger stability regions or admissible step sizes is unsupported.
issues.title: Claims of explicit-RK comparison and superior stability are not supported by the experiments
issues.why_classification: A complete repair requires substantial additional comparative experiments; the alternative is a material but limited withdrawal of the paper's competitiveness claims.
